paper_title: Heartbeat Thinking: Speculative Reasoning and Tool Execution While Listening in Realtime Voice Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Voice agents use external tools to retrieve information and
carry out requests that depend on actions beyond the con-
versation itself. For these tasks, producing a useful answer
requires both model computation and external execution,
which can leave users waiting after they finish speaking.
Conventional cascaded pipelines often place this preparation
after speech ends. Yet the information needed to begin
may arrive much earlier: an agent can identify an order
while the user is still describing a delivery concern. Prior
work has shown that reasoning and tool use can begin on
partial speech, allowing some of this preparation to take
place during listening (Zhou et al., 2022; Chiang et al., 2026;
Arora et al., 2026; Hooper et al., 2026). The opportunity
is to reduce how much work remains when the agent must
answer the complete request.
sections.content: Early preparation is useful only when it produces work that can be reused for the full request. tool call cannot be dispatched while its required arguments remain incomplete, even if the user has already provided enough information to construct them. SHANKS carries reasoning forward but bounds each generation episode by speech chunk, which can truncate unfinished tool-call arguments (Chiang et al., 2026). SIA incorporates new events by interrupting ongoing generation; although dispatched tools are managed separately, call may be interrupted before it is issued (Hooper et al., 2026). Frequent updates can therefore limit the uninterrupted time available to form complete call. The evolving request determines whether completed results remain useful: an early search may need revision when the user adds budget constraint. Stream RAG explores parallel retrieval and checks whether intermediate results can serve the final request (Arora et al., 2026). These considerations motivate preparation policy that allows computation to finish across speech updates while letting later input determine which results still apply. We therefore introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles new speech in subsequent invocations while allowing work already underway to finish (Figure 2). During listening, periodic Thinker invocations read the latest partial transcript and shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. Independent invocations can overlap: one can finish con1 ANT INTERNATIONAL RESEARCH Heartbeat Thinking structing tool call while another processes updated input. Requested tools execute asynchronously, and their returned results enter the shared record. Later invocations can use these results to resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls. Preparation can thus advance through successive reasoning and tool-use steps even when the transcript has not changed, without requiring each invocation to finish within an input-update window. To make this accumulated preparation useful for the final answer, Heartbeat separates speculative preparation from response generation. At the detected end of speech, Responder receives the complete request and the completed preparation available at the handoff. It checks completed work against the full request, reuses applicable results, and performs the remaining calls. Unfinished speculative jobs are cancelled at this handoff, allowing the Responder to begin without waiting for their completion. This explicit exchange of reasoning records and tool results also allows the Thinker and Responder to use independently selected models. Experiments on SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG show higher aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse than SHANKS-style Window Thinking. On FDBench v3, coverage increases from 34.67% to 50.67%, while mean final-response latency falls from 6.90 to 4.39 seconds (36.4%), also 45.7% below Pipecat, the fastest evaluated cascaded baseline. The coverage advantage persists across tested Responders. Task quality improves over Window Thinking on FDBench but decreases slightly on SpeechFCEval and AudioCRAG. Thus, computation spanning speech updates can increase reusable preparation and reduce final-response latency, while interpreting and using speculative results remains separate challenge.

sections.title:
5 Conclusion
Heartbeat Thinking overlaps speculative computation across
speech updates and passes completed preparation to a sepa-
rate Responder. Across three benchmarks, it retains more
reusable preparation than a SHANKS-style windowed base-
line; on FDBench, it also reduces final-response latency.
Task-quality changes vary by benchmark, highlighting the
importance of interpreting and using speculative results
correctly.
sections.content: Limitations Heartbeat uses fixed scheduling interval and bounded number of concurrent Thinker invocations. We have not explored adaptive scheduling based on changes in the partial transcript or the completion of tool calls. Such scheduling could reduce redundant inference when little new information is available. The Responder also receives snapshot of completed preparation at context assembly, excluding tool results returned afterward. Future work could explore incremental delivery of late results, particularly for tools with variable execution times. Finally, our latency analysis focuses on FDBench v3, and further evaluation across different tool workloads would help characterize the trade-off between speculative coverage, inference cost, and response latency. sections.title: A Detailed Framework
sections.content: A.1 Task and framework overview Let 𝑥 [0,𝑡 ] denote speech observed through time 𝑡, 𝐻 the dialogue history including tool calls and results from previous turns, and the available tool schemas. The current utterance ends at 𝑇. The task is to answer the complete request and execute its required tool calls using 𝐻, , and 𝑥 [0,𝑇 ]. Streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) provides partial transcripts during listening and final transcript of the complete utterance. Heartbeat separates preparation and response generation into two language-model roles (Figure 2). The Thinker is invoked periodically during listening to produce provisional reasoning and tool-call requests from partial transcripts. At the detected end of speech, speculative preparation stops and separate Responder is triggered. It uses the final transcript and the preparation already available to complete the remaining reasoning, tool calls, and final answer. Both roles receive 𝐻 and and may use different models. shared state stores current-turn preparation: completed Thinker outputs, their tool-call requests, and the associated results as they return. Tools execute asynchronously, independently of the model invocations. A.2 Periodic asynchronous Thinker Heartbeats occur at fixed interval Δ during listening, with at most 𝐾 Thinker invocations running concurrently. trigger is skipped rather than queued when 𝐾 invocations are already active. Otherwise, new invocation starts without interrupting earlier ones. An invocation started at 𝑡𝑘 receives 𝐻, , the latest partial transcript, completed outputs from earlier Thinker invocations in the current turn, and results from their tool calls available at 𝑡𝑘. New speech and newly returned tool results enter subsequent invocations rather than being injected into ongoing generation. The Thinker can produce three forms of output: no additional action, reasoning only, or reasoning with tool requests. These are encoded as noop, think without tool calls, and think with tool calls, respectively. noop indicates that the Thinker identifies no need for additional reasoning or tool requests given the current input and available preparation. Tool requests specify tool names and structured arguments once the necessary information is available. The prompt and output schema are given in Appendix G.1. Once think output is complete, its reasoning record and any tool-call requests are written to the shared state, after which the requested tools are dispatched asynchronously. Since one invocation may request multiple calls, tool concurrency is controlled separately from Thinker concurrency: dispatch imposes no concurrency limit, while the execution backend queues calls for execution. recorded call is pending until its result returns; the result is then linked to the request by its unique tool-call ID and stored alongside it. These records allow subsequent Thinker invocations to distinguish work already requested from results available for further reasoning. To avoid redundant calls, the prompt instructs each invocation not to repeat pending or completed 6 ANT INTERNATIONAL RESEARCH Heartbeat Thinking calls with the same tool name and complete arguments. Returned results can also supply new information for dependent calls, allowing preparation to advance even when the partial transcript is unchanged. A.3 Endpoint-triggered Responder The voice activity detection (VAD) module triggers the transition to response generation at the detected end of speech. At this point, the scheduler stops launching new Thinker invocations and cancels unfinished Thinker and speculative tool tasks, including queued calls. The Responder receives the final transcript, the shared history 𝐻, the tool schemas , and the preparation available at this transition. Let 𝑐 denote the VAD-triggered context-assembly time and 𝑎 𝑗 the availability time of preparation output 𝑟 𝑗 . The preparation snapshot is R𝑐 = {𝑟 𝑗 : 𝑟 𝑗 is complete and 𝑎 𝑗 𝑐}. (1) The snapshot contains completed Thinker records and returned tool results. completed record may include tool-call requests whose results are not yet available. Outputs returned by speculative jobs after 𝑐 are discarded. Appendix E.1 illustrates the boundary cases. The Responder follows ReAct process (Yao et al., 2023). It checks the preparation against the complete request and disregards interpretations contradicted by later speech. Its prompt directs it to reuse available results from completed calls that match the required operations in tool name and complete arguments. Required calls without available results, including those pending at the handoff, are issued by the Responder as part of its own ReAct process. Its system prompt and instructions for reading the Heartbeat context appear in Appendices G.2 and G.3. The answer can then be passed to text-to-speech, and the dialogue and retained tool-call records and results are carried forward to subsequent turns. Benchmark Setup For the main task-quality comparisons, the DeepSeek-V4Flash Responder uses the 0731 version. The cascaded pipelines combine Qwen3-ASR with text reasoning model. All experiments use NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Coverage and accuracy aggregation. For SpeechFCEval and FDBench, STC measures the fraction of reference calls covered by completed speculative calls whose results enter the Responder context without repetition by the Responder. Reference matching follows benchmark-specific tool-name and argument rules; repetition requires identical tool names and complete arguments. SpeechFCEval averages per-sample coverage, whereas FDBench aggregates over reference calls and checks repetitions across each recording. AudioCRAG STC measures the fraction of samples reusing completed speculative results without additional 7 retrieval. SpeechFCEval task accuracy requires correct function names and arguments and is averaged equally over its five task groups. combines B.1 SpeechFCEval SpeechFCEval from ACEBench and BFCL with SmartInteract (Tongyi Fun Team et al., 2026). It covers single and parallel function calling across synthesized and human speech. We evaluate the full test set. speech-based tasks The test set contains 1,914 samples: 208 and 88 in Speech-ACEBench single and parallel calling, 578 and 372 in Speech-BFCL single and parallel calling, and 668 in SmartInteract. All samples remain in the aggregate, with runtime failures contributing zero. Overall accuracy is averaged equally across the five task groups, while Overall STC is averaged across individual samples. The model comparisons use 500 ms heartbeat interval and at most two concurrent Thinker invocations. Thinking is disabled for the two Qwen Responders. B.2 FDBench v3 FDBench v3 tests whether voice agents follow spoken intent under disfluency (Lin et al., 2026). It evaluates turn taking, tool selection, argument accuracy, response quality, and task success. Spoken responses are transcribed for evaluation, and task performance is assessed from the executed calls and resulting answers. FDBench v3 contains 100 recordings covering 79 scenarios and 12 speakers. Spoken responses are transcribed with NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v2. We use DeepSeek-V4-Flash with maximum reasoning effort as the judge for FDBench v3. Quality follows the benchmark authors answer-quality assessment. For Heartbeat, Pass@1 requires completed speculative results and Responder calls jointly to fulfill the task without incorrect or extra Responder calls. The cascaded baselines use the same judge for argument accuracy, response quality, and Pass@1. Turn taking and tool selection follow the benchmarks original evaluation. Latency configuration. The latency evaluation uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the Thinker and DeepSeek-V4-Flash as the Responder, with thinking disabled for both models. Table 4 lists the speech components and timing settings. Latency protocol. Latencies are measured relative to each input turns aligned speech endpoint, excluding trailing silence. Final Response Latency measures the onset of the final spoken reply after the last tool call, or the onset of the reply when no tool call is required. sections.title: C Complete Results
sections.content: C.1 Task Results SpeechFCEval. Heartbeat achieves 43.69% STC, compared with 33.13% for the SHANKS-style Window Thinking baseline, an improvement of 10.56 percentage points. Across the five task groups reported in Table 6, coverage increases in four, with Speech-BFCL parallel calling improving from 36.34% to 58.03%. SmartInteract is the exception, where coverage decreases slightly from 40.57% to 38.32%. Despite achieving higher coverage, Heartbeat reaches 66.85% overall 8 function-calling accuracy, slightly below Window Thinking at 67.95%, although both outperform the cascaded baselines. This distinction indicates that retaining more speculative tool results does not necessarily improve function-calling accuracy. FDBench v3. Heartbeat achieves 50.67% STC, outperforming Window Thinkings 34.67% by 16.00 percentage points. Unlike SpeechFCEval, its task-quality scores also improve: Table 7 records an increase in response quality from 72.0% to 77.0% and in Pass@1 from 57.0% to 65.0%. These results show that Heartbeat retains more speculative tool work while achieving better task success than the windowed baseline under spoken disfluency. However, its Pass@1 remains below those of Speech-to-Speech and LiveKit. AudioCRAG. On AudioCRAG, Heartbeat reaches 62.42% STC but achieves correct-answer rate of 55.49%. The cascaded baselines listed in Table 8 achieve correct-answer rates between 56.48% and 59.45%. Window Thinking achieves 20.05% STC and 57.24% correct-answer rate. Heartbeats missing-answer rate increases from Window Thinkings 14.33% to 16.84%. This contrast further illustrates that higher speculative retrieval reuse does not guarantee better answer quality. The benefit of early retrieval depends not only on retaining completed results but also on whether the Responder can use them correctly. C.2 Model Comparisons We vary the Thinker and Responder separately to test preparation and reuse across models. Thinker choice. All four Thinkers achieve nonzero STC on all three benchmarks (Tables 68). Higher coverage does not consistently yield better task performance: on SpeechFCEval, Gemma achieves higher accuracy than the default Thinker (68.58% vs. 66.85%) despite slightly lower STC (42.71% vs. 43.69%). Responder choice. Heartbeat retains higher STC than Window Thinking with all three Responders on all three benchmarks, including FDBench  (Table 3)  . However, model rankings differ by metric: on SpeechFCEval, Qwen3.8Flash-Next achieves higher STC than Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (55.27% vs. 41.20%) but lower accuracy (64.30% vs. 69.70%). sections.title: E Scheduling and Coverage Details
sections.content: E.1 Overlapping jobs and the response boundary tool call dispatched during listening contributes its result to the initial Responder context when the result is complete and available at context assembly 𝑐 (Equation 1). At the detected end of speech, the scheduler stops launching new Thinker invocations and cancels unfinished Thinker and speculative tool tasks, including queued calls. Later results are excluded from the current response. At context assembly, completed Thinker record may be available even if its requested tool result is unavailable. Overlapping invocations can finish out of order. E.2 Interpreting speculative tool coverage Each reference call contributes at most once to requests coverage fraction. The denominator is the number of referANT INTERNATIONAL RESEARCH Heartbeat Thinking Figure 5: Speculative tool calls during listening on FDBench v3. Red markers indicate the last words available to the Thinker when each invocation began; callouts give tool-request initiation times and arguments. Times are relative to audio onset. Word alignment is approximate, and ASR text is normalized for display. ence calls; repeated speculative attempts cannot contribute multiple matches to the same reference call. Matching reference and detecting Responder repetition are separate tests. The first establishes relevance under the benchmarks matching rule, while the second removes retained coverage when the Responder makes call with the same tool name and exactly the same arguments. Suppose request requires two calls. Both speculative results are completed and injected, but the Responder repeats one with identical arguments. The requests non-repeated coverage is 1/2. If one result instead arrives after context assembly and the other is not repeated, the coverage is also 1/2, but the loss now occurs at the preparation boundary rather than through response-time repetition.

sections.title: F Extended Related Work
sections.content: Incremental reasoning and response preparation. Preparation from partial input can target intermediate reasoning, candidate responses, or both. LiveMind stores prefix-based inferences in memory for subsequent reasoning and final response generation (Chen et al., 2024). PredGen instead drafts candidate responses, verifies reusable prefixes as input grows, and prepares audio for the first sentence (Li and Grover, 2025). LTS-VoiceAgent combines these forms of preparation: its Thinker maintains corrected transcripts, key variables, and plans, while its Speaker uses this state to begin solving and generating responses before speech ends (Zou et al., 2026). The prepared content therefore ranges from reasoning context for later generation to response text and audio that can be reused directly. Scheduling speculative computation under streaming input. Early tool execution was studied in online semantic parsing through prefix-to-program prediction and selective subprogram execution (Zhou et al., 2022). Subsequent systems differ in how computation proceeds as input changes. SHANKS interleaves speech chunks with reasoning and tool calls, but its per-chunk generation budget can leave long call arguments incomplete (Chiang et al., 2026, Appendix C.2). Stream RAG contrasts fixed-interval parallel retrieval with model-triggered queries that terminate unfinished calls for In Speculative the previous query (Arora et al., 2026). Interaction Agents (SIA), incoming user or tool updates interrupt ongoing generation, potentially before complete tool call is produced, while dispatched tools are managed separately (Hooper et al., 2026). Outside speech, PASTE predicts upcoming calls from recurring execution patterns and starts them while the LLM is still generating (Sui et al., 2026). Heartbeat allows successive Thinker invocations to overlap within concurrency limit. This supports denser triggers without making the next input update deadline for ongoing generation. Decoupled architectures and coordination interfaces. Decoupled systems use different interfaces to pass intermediate work between components. The SHANKS + call-after11 ANT INTERNATIONAL RESEARCH Heartbeat Thinking listen configuration passes successful calls and their results to model that processes the complete request (Chiang et al., 2026). DuplexOmni separates real-time interaction from background reasoning and tool use, returning intermediate outputs through streaming interface (Huang et al., 2026). Other interfaces operate within the models generation process: AsyncLM encodes tool calls and returned results in the token stream (Gim et al., 2024), whereas AsyncReasoning coordinates thinker and writer views through shared modelinternal attention state (Yakushev et al., 2025). Heartbeat connects independent Thinker invocations, asynchronous tool jobs, and an endpoint-triggered Responder through completed reasoning records and tool results. This external interface permits independent model selection and modulelevel optimization without requiring shared model-internal state. Modular Prompt Assembly The following blocks show the shared Thinker and Responder instructions and their message roles. Benchmark-specific instructions, tool schemas, dialogue history, and current-turn state are represented by placeholders. G.1 Thinker prompt The Thinker system message declares its role; the user message assembles the fixed preparation rules and variable modules. SYSTEM You are an incremental HeartBeat Thinking worker for general real-time voice assistant. USER [Task] Work speculatively from the current cumulative partial ASR transcript while the user is speaking. Preserve useful incremental interpretations and propose supported tool calls. You do not answer the user directly. Response will independently interpret the complete final input. [Tools] <Benchmark tool schemas> [Decision policy] - Return noop when there is neither useful new interpretation nor newly actionable tool call. Repeated speech may still permit new call when completed result has supplied missing dependency. - Otherwise return think, with one concise incremental operational note and any eligible calls. new stable intent with missing arguments can produce thinking with an empty tools array. note that merely says to wait adds no useful interpretation. - Do not propose call identical to an existing pending or status-completed HB call. This does not depend on result content or answer sufficiency. call with different arguments remains eligible when supported by the current request, not merely to bypass this rule. [Argument rules] - Copy the exact supplied tool name and schemadefined argument keys. Satisfy required fields , JSON types, enums, and stated preconditions; do not invent tools, fields, or capabilities. - Support values with the current transcript, unambiguous conversation history, or relevant usable completed results. Do not invent missing facts or fill required fields with placeholders. [Output format (STRICT)] Return one JSON object. {"action":"noop"} or {"action":"think","thinking":"...","tools":[{"name ":"...","arguments":{...}}]} Use an empty array when there is no tool call. No markdown fences, no explanation, no extra keys. Tool schemas are also passed through the structured tool interface. SYSTEM You are continuing work in an existing assistant turn, not starting the users request over. HeartbeatContext records work already performed for this turn. Its thinking is speculative: retain useful interpretations, but do not treat intentions as commands, proof of execution, or evidence for missing arguments.
